title.narrative: IWRM 4 WASH A Market-based Approach

description.narrative: Inception phaseIn year one (October 2019-July 2021), the project will undertake a number of activities geared towards setting a strong foundation for effective project implementation. Key activities that will be prioritized during this phase include defining the project scope and gaining stakeholder consensus; developing a detailed implementation plan with the key strategic partners, conducting a baseline assessment to establish the project benchmarks; developing a project risk and mitigation plan, handling all logistical and administrative requirements and exemptions necessary for smooth project implementation and setting up the monitoring and evaluation system. - This phase would pursue the case study, action-learning, and networking components in parallel. Implementation phaseImplementation of the anticipated follow-up project (component 2) is estimated to take four years (July 2021 - December 2025). The outputs of activities for component one (the inception phase) will determine the extent and scope of the second phase of the Project. Hence, the detailed activities needing external funding will be further defined after the end of the first phase.

Integrated Water Resources Management for Water Sanitation and Hygiene is a Market-based approachThe project will be implemented in Ethiopia, focusing on the water catchment areas surrounding Addis Ababa in the Oromia Regional State. It will specifically target the four main surface water supply sources for Addis Ababa: the Legedadi, Gefersa, Dire, and Akaki catchments, along with their associated reservoirs. Additionally, the project will extend to five nearby towns within and around these catchment areas: Akaki, Burayu, Gelan, Sululta, and Sendafa.

name.narrative: Upper Awash Basin – Oromia and Addis Ababa (Dire, Adere, Legedadi, Sululta, Sendafa, Gelan, Akaki)

description.narrative: The IWRM4WASH project operates across the Upper Awash Basin, mainly within Oromia Regional State and Addis Ababa’s water catchment zones. The program integrates water resource management, WASH service expansion, and livelihood initiatives. Core intervention areas include Adere and Legedadi catchments for watershed rehabilitation; and the towns of Sululta, Sendafa, Gelan, Akaki, and Burayu for improved water and sanitation services.

activity-description.narrative: Between 2021 and 2024, the project implemented a mix of watershed rehabilitation, WASH infrastructure construction, and utility capacity development. Key outputs include the rehabilitation of 925.7 ha of degraded land, sediment reduction by 30%, construction of reservoirs and sanitation facilities benefiting over 165,000 people, and digitalization of utility billing systems. Activities are implemented through VEI in partnership with AAWSA, OWERDB, and local utilities.

policy-marker.narrative: Gender equality and women’s participation were mainstreamed across project activities.Women represented about 45 % of training participants and over 50 % of irrigation and catchment groups.Gender-sensitive WASH infrastructure (separate and disability-friendly toilets) was implemented in Sendafa and Gelan.

The project directly contributes to climate-change adaptation by promoting integrated watershed management, soil and water conservation, and reforestation that reduce erosion and strengthen ecosystem resilience inthe Upper Awash Basin.
The project strengthens governance through trans-regional dialogue between AAWSA, OWERDB, and MoWIE, and by empowering local utilities and communities in joint watershed and WASH planning.

2025 Improved reservoir protection and catchment rehabilitation through IWRM interventions

description.narrative: Between 2021 and 2025, the IWRM4WASH project implemented large scale soil and water conservation interventions in the Adere, Dire, and Legedadi catchments to protect key water supply reservoirs serving Addis Ababa and Sheger towns.By the end of 2025, a total of 1,098.56 ha of degraded land had been rehabilitated, exceeding the original target of 1,037 ha. The interventions included terraces, check dams, gully treatments, area closures, grass planting, afforestation, and other biological measures. The 2025 hectare verification confirmed the cumulative achievement and demonstrated the project’s strong progress in restoring degraded catchment areas.The erosion control assessment showed that soil loss in the Adere watershed declined significantly compared with the 2021 baseline, confirming the positive impact of the project’s integrated soil and water conservation measures. The project also continued to strengthen biological restoration through seedling planting, while the masonry dam and solar powered irrigation system supported local livelihood opportunities, including job creation for youth and improved agricultural productivity.Implementation was guided by joint planning and coordination with AAWSA, OWERDB, the Bureau of Agriculture, local administrations, and watershed committees. This helped strengthen local ownership, improve coordination between upstream and downstream stakeholders, and support the integration of catchment protection measures into the wider Upper Awash catchment management framework.

title.narrative: In 2025, the IWRM4WASH project consolidated and completed its Soil and Water Conservation interventions in the Adere watershed, Dire catchment, and Legedadi catchment, building on the substantial progress achieved in previous years.An additional 172.86 hectares of degraded land were treated in 2025, bringing the cumulative rehabilitated area to 1,098.56 hectares. This represents approximately 106% of the overall project target of 1,037 hectares, meaning the project exceeded its original land rehabilitation target.The 2025 hectare verification confirmed the rehabilitated areas through physical measurement, GPS data collection, GIS mapping, and visual inspection of Soil and Water Conservation structures and vegetative cover. The verification process ensured that the reported achievements were accurate, traceable, and supported by field based evidence.The verification was jointly conducted by VEI, AAWSA, local watershed experts, and relevant local stakeholders. This joint process strengthened transparency, ownership, and confidence in the reported rehabilitation achievements, while also supporting the integration of catchment protection measures into the broader Upper Awash catchment management framework.

title.narrative: Strengthened trans-regional dialogue and coordination for Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM) in the Upper Awash Basin

description.narrative: During the final year of the project, the transregional dialogue continued to strengthen coordination and shared ownership among institutions responsible for water-resource management and service delivery. Stakeholders included AAWSA, OWERDB, MoWIE, Sheger City utilities, woreda administrations, agriculture offices, and VEI.In 2025, the dialogue focused on reviewing project progress and identifying arrangements for sustaining results beyond the project period. Discussions and technical exchanges addressed the integration of watershed protection and IWRM principles into regular utility operations, continued cooperation between upstream and downstream stakeholders, non-revenue water, service reliability, and the maintenance of project-supported interventions without external financing.The end-term evaluation confirmed that improved coordination between water-resource institutions and service-delivery organizations was an important project contribution. By the end of 2025, the dialogue had developed from a project-based coordination mechanism into an established working relationship, providing a foundation for continued institutional collaboration on source-water protection and improved water services after project closure.

title.narrative: Number of trans-regional dialogue meetings conducted in 2024

description.narrative: This indicator tracks the number of high-level trans-regional dialogue meetings convened in 2024 to strengthen coordination between Addis Ababa Water and Sewerage Authority (AAWSA), Oromia Water and Energy Resources Development Bureau (OWERDB), Basin Development Authority (BDA), and other key institutions working on Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM) in the Upper Awash Basin.In 2024, one high-level trans-regional dialogue was successfully conducted in Addis Ababa.Although the original logframe envisioned two dialogues per year, this proved overly ambitious given the executive nature of the meetings, which require cross-institutional scheduling, approvals, and high-level representation.To maintain momentum, the project organized multiple mid-level stakeholder forums and technical consultations throughout the year. These sessions engaged over 60 experts and decision-makers from federal, regional, and utility institutions to review project progress, share IWRM best practices, and align planning for watershed rehabilitation, WASH integration, and policy coordination.The 2024 dialogue reaffirmed institutional collaboration and strengthened consensus around the Strategic Framework for Trans-Regional Cooperation, which is being finalized for joint adoption in 2025.

title.narrative: Institutional collaboration and trans-regional dialogue established for integrated water resource management.

description.narrative: The IWRM4WASH project strengthened cooperation among AAWSA, OWERDB, MoWIE, Basin Development Authority (BDA), BoA, Sheger City Administration, and VEI to promote coordinated catchment management across administrative boundaries.During the inception phase (Dec 2020), a baseline validation workshop was convened that brought these key institutions together for the first time to validate the biophysical and socio-economic baseline results and to agree on shared IWRM priorities. This meeting laid the foundation for formalized trans-regional coordination under Result 1.Between 2021 and 2024, regular technical consultations and stakeholder fora were conducted to maintain coordination and share progress. In 2024, one executive-level trans-regional dialogue was successfully held, engaging all major institutions and EKN, leading to joint understanding of IWRM–WASH linkages and commitments for sustained collaboration.

title.narrative: Expanded access to safe water and sanitation services in Burayu, Sululta, Sendafa, Gelan and Akaki through improved utility capacity and inclusive infrastructure.

description.narrative: From 2021 to 2025, the IWRM4WASH project expanded access to safe and reliable water and sanitation services across Burayu, Sululta, Sendafa, Gelan and Akaki. Investments included the construction and rehabilitation of water-storage reservoirs, network improvements, sanitation facilities, operational support and capacity strengthening for participating utilities.By project completion, at least 165,750 people had benefited from improved WASH infrastructure and services. The interventions increased water-storage capacity, expanded service coverage, improved reliability and strengthened the ability of utilities to operate and maintain the supported systems. The project also promoted inclusive access by considering the needs of underserved and rapidly growing urban and peri-urban communities.

title.narrative: Gender equality, youth participation, climate resilience and knowledge management integrated across IWRM and WASH interventions

description.narrative: From 2021 to 2025, the project integrated gender equality, youth participation, climate resilience and knowledge management across its IWRM and WASH activities. Women and young people participated in watershed rehabilitation, livelihood activities, community mobilisation, training and local management arrangements. Climate-resilient measures included soil and water conservation, catchment restoration, source-water protection, water-efficiency improvements and livelihood activities designed to reduce pressure on rehabilitated areas. Project experience, technical findings and lessons learned were documented and shared through stakeholder dialogue, assessments, reports and practical knowledge products to support continued application beyond the project period.The project integrated gender equity, youth participation, climate resilience, and knowledge sharing into both watershed and WASH interventions.

title.narrative: Climate risks to Addis Ababa’s urban water infrastructure assessed and adaptation pathways developed

description.narrative: In 2025, the project completed a climate-risk assessment covering Addis Ababa and the surrounding catchments supplying the Dire, Legedadi and Gefersa reservoirs. The study analysed historical temperature and rainfall trends, future climate projections, meteorological and hydrological drought, and the potential impacts of climate change on reservoirs, groundwater, water quality, sewerage, drainage and water-service infrastructure.The assessment also reviewed AAWSA’s Water Safety Plan and Climate-Resilient Water Safety Plan and identified practical adaptation pathways. Recommendations included watershed restoration, nature-based solutions, groundwater-recharge protection, reservoir and sediment management, improved stormwater systems, reduction of non-revenue water, climate-resilient infrastructure, stronger institutional coordination and sustainable climate financing. The study provides evidence to support climate-informed planning and future investment in Addis Ababa’s urban water system.

title.narrative: 2025 Livelihoods and food security enhanced through adaptive, community-based approaches supporting catchment restoration and access improvement.

description.narrative: The livelihood component of the IWRM4WASH project was initially designed to pilot a market based approach by linking conservation incentives to microfinance supported enterprises. However, due to limited engagement from local MFIs and limited community uptake of loan based support, this approach was not implemented as originally envisioned.In 2025, the project continued with a more practical and adaptive livelihood model closely linked to watershed rehabilitation. The fruit farm established near the masonry dam became more productive, supported by solar powered irrigation, vegetable production, beekeeping, and improved site management. The site continued to provide regular work opportunities for more than 30 youth and served as a visible example of how watershed protection can also support local income generation.The project also strengthened livelihood support through seedling production and plantation activities, cattle trough construction, hydroponics demonstration, and continued support to the nursery youth group. Across the full project period, more than 1,650 individuals benefited directly from livelihood related interventions.Although the original microfinance based model and full training targets were not achieved as planned, the adapted livelihood approach delivered practical results by creating local employment, supporting household resilience, improving livestock water access, and strengthening community ownership of watershed restoration activities.

description.narrative: The IWRM4WASH project strengthened cooperation among AAWSA, OWERDB, MoWIE, Basin Development Authority (BDA), BoA, Sheger City Administration, and VEI to promote coordinated catchment management across administrative boundaries.During the inception phase (Dec 2020), a baseline validation workshop was convened that brought these key institutions together for the first time to validate the biophysical and socio-economic baseline results and to agree on shared IWRM priorities. This meeting laid the foundation for formalized trans-regional coordination under Result 1.Between 2021 and 2024, regular technical consultations and stakeholder fora were conducted to maintain coordination and share progress. In 2024, one executive-level trans-regional dialogue was successfully held, engaging all major institutions and EKN, leading to joint understanding of IWRM–WASH linkages and commitments for sustained collaboration.
